articles.title: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law
articles.summary: A film broadcast by Channel 4 shows senior Reform UK figures discussing donations with an undercover reporter.
articles.body:
Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4.

Dan Jukes was filmed meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American businessman.

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.

The undercover filming was done by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.

Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".

The reporter posing as the son of the American donor is filmed raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Filmed standing outside a pub in Westminster, Jukes said "you do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

"Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

"That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.

Reform UK have launched an internal investigation into Jukes. They would not confirm if he remained a party spokesperson.

Later, Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with both the reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor – his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Dan Jukes and the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's Head of Policy, James Orr about it for some time.

"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."

"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.

Orr is also now the subject of an internal Reform UK investigation.

Earlier in Channel 4 News's film, prior to the suggested half a million pound donation, Channel 4 says Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps his father could pay for opinion polling to aide Reform's campaigning.

The poll would cost £18,000 plus VAT – and Orr suggests that perhaps the polling company could send the bill to the undercover reporter.

In all, Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.

Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.

A Reform spokesperson said: "Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The party denies any wrongdoing.

"Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission.

"The hoaxers are 'Verbatim Investigations'; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Center for Climate Reporting (CCR). The methods of its founder, Lawrence Carter, have previously been rebuked by members of the United States Congress for videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation."

An Electoral Commission spokesperson said: "The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500.

"Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."

A spokesman for the Metropolitan Police told the BBC: "We're aware of media reporting on Thursday, 3 September involving political party donations and an alleged breach of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 relating to polling. We will assess this matter and any information provided to us."

It is understood the force has not begun an investigation.

articles.title: Don’t share any sensitive tech with Pak, Rajnath asks Belgian minister; both countries ink 10 defence pacts on rockets, military hardware
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh Thursday made it clear to visiting Belgian defence minister and trade minister Theo Francken that for Indo-B.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh Thursday made it clear to visiting Belgian defence minister and trade minister Theo Francken that for Indo-Belgian defence relations to flourish, his country should not have any defence pact on sensitive technology with Pakistan. The Belgian defence minister agreed to India’s request.“In response to defence minister Rajnath Singh asking the Belgian defence minister to keep India’s sensitivity in mind regarding transfer of sensitive technology to Pakistan during their meeting on Thursday morning, the Belgian minister responded that they are clear in their mind and they have chosen India without any doubt in mind,” a defence source told TOI.Francken also made it clear “till the time he is the defence minister of Belgium, there is no question of any cooperation with Pakistan”.The source also TOI that the Belgian minister’s reply is “similar to the response from the Italian defence minister (Guido Crosetto when he met Rajnath on April 30) and this shows that European countries have clearly chosen India (over Pakistan), vindicating India’s stance”.After the meeting, Rajnath said on X, “We reviewed the entire spectrum of defence relations and defence industrial cooperation between India and Belgium. Multiple MoUs and contracts under the defence industrial cooperation were also signed, towards leveraging Belgian technology together with Indian skill and scale.” India and Belgium inked a defence framework pact and separately, 10 pacts on collaboration between Belgian and Indian defence industries were signed, involving production of Belgian military hardware such as rockets in India.The Belgian side said that “there are also opportunities (to have cooperation with India) in weapon systems, ammunition, radar, electro-optical sensors, command and control, and counter-drone systems. These are precisely areas in which Belgian industry has particularly strong expertise.”“With this visit, we are reaping the benefits of what we have built over the past year. Every project that connects our technology with India’s growing defence industry strengthens both our security and economic position,” Francken said.At the India-Belgium Defence CEOs Roundtable and B2B meetings attended by MoS defence Sanjay Seth, Francken emphasised the strong potential for deeper industrial collaboration between the two sides to strengthen the defence forces through collective efforts. The Belgium defence minister underscored the growing strategic partnership between India and the European Union (EU), highlighting the robust dialogue structures developing across maritime security, information security and aerospace. He stated that these institutional frameworks have established India as a trusted partner for the EU.Commending the dynamism of Indian entrepreneurs, Francken stressed the need to bolster the two militaries in the evolving security environment through joint efforts. “United we stand, divided we fall,” he said.Seth urged Belgian defence manufacturers to leverage their technological expertise alongside India’s manufacturing scale for co-development and co-production of niche products for shared security and prosperity. Highlighting the strategic transformation of India’s defence manufacturing sector, MoS defence stated that the nation is decisively moving from import dependence to indigenous capability, trusted partnerships, and global competitiveness through initiatives such as Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make-in-India. “This transformation is outward-facing. Strategic autonomy is best secured through credible, mutually beneficial international collaboration,” he said.Seth emphasised that India and Belgium can leverage their strengths and prioritise collaboration in areas including cyber security, AI-enabled unmanned aerial systems, underwater domain vehicles, and complex weapon systems.In a related development, global defence major Thales and Kalyani Strategic Systems Ltd (KSSL), a subsidiary of India’s Bharat Forge, have signed a “strategic alliance agreement” to explore collaboration on both unguided and laser-guided variants of Thales’ combat-proven 70-mm rocket systems to help enhance the operational readiness of the Indian armed forces, officials said on Thursday. Thales Belgium is a 100% subsidiary of Thales Group.The alliance provides a framework for technology transfer, local production and distribution for both unguided and laser-guided 70-mm rocket systems and associated equipment. The collaboration aims to develop a robust local supply chain and position India as a strategic manufacturing and export hub for advanced rocket systems. The first fully assembled rocket produced in India is targeted for early 2027.

articles.title: El Nino: A phenomenon supercharged by climate change
articles.summary: Scientists warn the 2026-27 El Nino could become the strongest ever, exacerbating global heat, droughts and floods.
articles.body:
Anchovies are an unlikely bellwether for a building climatic event, but their disappearance from the coast of South America is heralding one of the biggest El Ninos in living memory.

These small fish usually live in colossal shoals along the Pacific coast of South America, feeding in the cold, nutrient-rich waters. Fishermen in Peru and Chile eagerly await the fishing season every year, but every now and then, it does not come as planned. This is one of those years.

Some years the easterly trade winds in the Pacific weaken or even reverse. The trigger for this remains uncertain, but it causes a warm ocean current to flow east to the coast of South America. This replaces the nutrient-rich cold water, causing the anchovies to disappear.

Because the warm waters arrive around Christmas time, Peruvian fishermen named the phenomenon El Nino de Navidad (The Christmas Child).

The impact of El Nino, a natural weather pattern, spreads much further than South America, and can bring drought or floods to millions in affected areas. This year it comes supercharged by climate change, which is worrying many scientists, governments and aid workers.

Stephanie Roe, lead climate scientist with the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), told Al Jazeera that this “super El Nino” is a stark reminder of how climate change can intensify pressures on both people and the natural world.

“El Nino can bring devastating climate extremes on its own, but it’s unfolding today on a much warmer planet, increasing the likelihood that heat, drought, floods and fires will push communities and ecosystems beyond anything they have experienced before,” Roe said.

As it develops in the Pacific, this year’s El Nino is combining with an ongoing, massive marine heatwave, further adding to the impacts of human-induced global warming. Its effects will be felt through food systems and biodiversity, impacting the livelihoods of fishermen and farmers, and the billions around the world reliant on the agricultural industry for their food.

El Nino’s development is being closely monitored from both space and sea, using satellites and a network of buoys. The devices in the Pacific Ocean continuously transmit data on ocean temperatures , currents and winds, helping scientists assess how powerful the event could become. Indications currently suggest the 2026-27 El Nino could be the strongest on record.

Research by the Met Office, the United Kingdom’s national weather and climate service, shows that a typical El Nino episode leads to temperature rises of between 1 and 2 degrees Celsius in the equatorial Pacific Ocean. But projections now indicate that when El Nino fully bites in late 2026 or early 2027, temperatures could spike by 3C.

“We should be clear this is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Nino signal this intense in our forecasts,” Adam Scaife, professor and the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, told Al Jazeera.

“This implies that if the forecast is accurate – and other forecast systems show similar extreme values – then this will far exceed our recent experience of El Nino and its worldwide climate influences,” Scaife said.

Scientists know that the weather is never certain, but an El Nino ramped up by global warming spells trouble. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has compared it to “pouring fuel on the fire of a warming world”.

The effects will be felt by billions across the world, bringing droughts to some regions and severe flooding to others. In some cases, it can bring both.

Southeast Asia and South America will be particularly badly affected by this phenomenon, according to Carbon Brief, a United Kingdom-based website specialising in climate issues. There might be drought in Southern Africa, but flooding in the east of the continent. El Nino could also bring extreme heat that would weaken summer monsoons, leading to drought.

According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, this super El Nino demands exceptional preparation and response. “Never before in the 50-year history of the WMO have we launched such a major mobilisation delivering forecasts and services to save lives and livelihoods,” she said.

El Ninos can reduce the number and size of Atlantic hurricanes and provide welcome rainfall to drought-stricken areas. Models indicate that the peak will be from December to February, which coincides with the main planting season and crop-development period in South America.

Investment bank Morgan Stanley said that wetter conditions could benefit agricultural yields in Argentina and southern Brazil, but other parts of Brazil might face more irregular rainfall and delayed planting.

Overall, the outlook is grim, with crop failures caused by El Nino and the climate crisis rippling through supply chains and leading to billions of dollars in damage to the global economy. One group of economists at Citigroup investment bank have estimated that a super El Nino could inflict as much as $7 trillion in global economic losses over five years, as its effects leave lasting scars on gross domestic product (GDP) growth.

“Most El Nino years are a nuisance, but this one has the makings of a shock, as weather patterns shift across key growing regions,” said Julia Rizzo, Morgan Stanley’s commodities strategist for Latin America.

“The effects may extend far beyond local forecasts and into supply chains, prices and investment returns.”

The World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that El Nino could hit as global food systems face systemic challenges due to high energy and fertiliser prices, brought about by the United States’ war on Iran .

“Together these factors increase the risk that climate shocks could push more people into hunger,” the WFP told Al Jazeera.

The United Nations agency forecasts that 274 million people will be facing acute hunger by the end of 2027, an increase of 49 million from current levels.

Outbreaks of disease, like malaria and dengue fever, could be another consequence, particularly in places where sanitation and health systems are already under pressure.

John Nairn, WMO’s senior extreme heat adviser, said extreme heat is the most direct concern.

“Where pre-existing drought exists, heatwaves intensify and compound other hazards such as water scarcity, dust, wildfires, smoke and flash floods,” Nairn said. “Each carries its own burden, ranging from heat mortality and respiratory impacts to waterborne disease.”

It is also feared that the compounding effects of El Nino will put highly stressed ecosystems under more pressure.

In the Pacific region, the loss of baitfish, including anchovies and sardines, is having a knock-on effect up the food chain and could cause deaths among seals and sea lions. Thousands of seabirds have also already washed up dead on Eastern Pacific coasts from California to Ecuador.

“Our recent surveys have been reporting seabird strandings and deaths every day, but it started to explode in June. It showcases the magnitude of this El Nino over such a large expanse of the Pacific,” said Sebastian Cruz of the American Bird Conservancy.

And perhaps most alarming of all for scientists is the likely increase in global temperatures.

“During large El Nino events, significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere, leading to an increase in global average temperature,” said Met Office climate scientist Nick Dunstone. “So 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the hottest year on record.”

articles.title: A 12.5-mile pipeline supplied water to the Grand Canyon, now a deadly flood has damaged the lifeline, threatening the park’s 6 million annual visitors
articles.summary: For decades, a single 12.5-mile pipeline has carried water across the arid landscape of northern Arizona to the South Rim of the Grand Canyon, sustain.
articles.body: For decades, a single 12.5-mile pipeline has carried water across the arid landscape of northern Arizona to the South Rim of the Grand Canyon, sustaining lodges, campgrounds, restaurants and restrooms for one of the world’s most visited national parks. In late August 2026, a sudden, deadly flash flood tore through the pipeline’s route, rupturing sections of the line and cutting off a major portion of the park’s water supply. With about 6 million visitors expected this year, the damage threatens not only daily operations but also the safety and comfort of guests in one of the most remote tourist destinations on Earth. As reported by The Associated Press, park officials are racing to repair the line while imposing strict water restrictions and preparing for a long, complicated recovery.The pipeline that keeps the canyon runningThe Grand Canyon’s South Rim sits at more than 7,000 feet elevation, surrounded by high desert with limited natural water sources. To meet the needs of millions of visitors and hundreds of employees, the National Park Service relies on a network of wells, storage tanks and, crucially, a 12.5-mile pipeline that transports water from Roaring Springs, north of the park, to the main developed areas along the rim.This pipeline is the park’s lifeline. It supplies water to: hotels and lodges where visitors stay overnight; restaurants, gift shops and visitor centres; campgrounds, restrooms and shower facilities; and fire suppression systems and other critical infrastructure.Without it, the South Rim cannot operate at anything close to normal capacity.A flash flood with deadly consequencesOn August 28, 2026, a powerful storm system moved across the region, dumping heavy rain on already saturated ground. In the park and surrounding areas, dry washes and creeks swelled into raging torrents. Tragically, at least one person died in flood-related incidents, and several others were rescued from dangerous situations.Along the pipeline’s route, the floodwaters did more than rise; they scoured the ground, uprooting vegetation, moving large debris and changing the shape of stream channels. In several places, the force of the water exposed, bent or broke sections of the buried pipeline. When park crews inspected the line, they found multiple ruptures and leaks that had already begun draining valuable water into the desert.Immediate impact on park operationsWith the pipeline damaged, the Grand Canyon’s water system lost a significant portion of its supply almost overnight. Park officials responded by implementing emergency water restrictions across the South Rim: lodges and restaurants were asked to limit laundry, dishwashing and other non-essential uses; some restrooms and shower facilities were closed or operated on reduced schedules; and visitors were urged to shorten their stays, bring their own water and be prepared for limited services.In some cases, water had to be trucked in to critical facilities, an expensive and logistically challenging stopgap. Park staff also began coordinating with nearby communities and tribal nations to explore additional temporary water sources.Repairs in a remote, rugged landscapeFixing the pipeline is not as simple as sending out a repair crew. Much of the line runs through remote, rugged terrain with limited road access, making it difficult to bring in heavy equipment, replacement pipe and construction crews. After the flood, some access roads were themselves damaged or washed out, further complicating the effort.Park engineers and contractors must locate all damaged sections, some of which may be buried under debris or sediment. They should also excavate carefully to avoid causing additional harm to the surrounding landscape, replace or reinforce pipe segments, then test the system for leaks before restoring full flow.Weather remains a wildcard. Another storm could delay work, damage newly repaired sections or create new hazards for crews working in washes and along steep slopes.Why the pipeline is so vulnerableThe Grand Canyon water pipeline was built decades ago, in an era when climate patterns were more stable and extreme weather events were less frequent. Its route was chosen based on the best available data at the time, but it crosses numerous washes and flood-prone areas that have become more dangerous as storms intensify.Park officials acknowledge that the flood damage is likely a preview of future challenges. As the region warms and atmospheric rivers and monsoon storms grow more volatile, infrastructure like this pipeline will face greater stress. Long-term solutions may include: rerouting sections of the pipeline away from high-risk washes; burying pipe deeper or reinforcing it with additional protection; and building redundant systems so that a single failure does not cripple the entire park.But all of these options are costly and time-consuming, and they must be balanced against other pressing needs in a park that already struggles with aging infrastructure.What it means for visitorsFor the millions of people who visit the Grand Canyon each year, the pipeline damage is a stark reminder of how fragile services can be in remote natural areas. Many visitors assume that lodges, restaurants and restrooms will function as they would in a city, but the reality is that everything depends on a small number of critical systems in a harsh environment.During the repair period, visitors are being asked to: bring more water than they think they will need, especially if hiking or camping; be prepared for limited restroom and shower access; expect possible changes to lodging and dining availability; and follow all park guidance and closures, particularly around flooded areas and damaged infrastructure.Park officials stress that the Grand Canyon remains open, but that conditions are fluid and can change quickly.A broader lesson for national parksThe Grand Canyon’s water crisis echoes challenges facing other national parks across the West, where aging infrastructure meets a changing climate. From Yellowstone to Yosemite, parks are dealing with:Roads and bridges damaged by floods and landslides.Water and sewer systems stressed by higher visitation and more extreme weather.Power and communication lines vulnerable to storms and wildfires.The Grand Canyon pipeline incident underscores the need for sustained investment in park infrastructure, not just for visitor comfort but for safety and resilience. It also highlights the importance of planning for a future in which “once-in-a-century” storms may become far more common.Looking aheadIn the short term, the focus is on getting the pipeline back in service and restoring normal water supply to the South Rim. In the longer term, the park will have to decide how much to invest in hardening this critical lifeline against future floods and whether to develop additional redundancy in its water system.For now, the 12.5-mile pipeline remains a symbol of both human ingenuity and vulnerability: a thin blue line across the desert that keeps a world-famous park running, and a reminder that even the most iconic places depend on infrastructure that a single, violent storm can break.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Burnham, Macron talk border security and stronger Europe-UK ties
articles.summary: New UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham discussed shared challenges in his first official meeting with the French president.
articles.body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron have held talks about migration, the war in Ukraine and trade during an official meeting in London.

The talks, held at Burnham’s Downing Street office on Thursday, marked the first time the prime minister has hosted a European leader since taking over the reins from former Labour Party leader Keir Starmer on July 20.

Burnham and Macron discussed shared challenges, including small boat crossings and the “emerging use of mega dinghies” transporting undocumented migrants and asylum seekers to England’s south coast, according to a United Kingdom government press release.

Downing Street said the UK saw the lowest number of small boat arrivals since 2020, but “the government will not stop bearing down on the criminal gangs facilitating the dangerous crossings”, the statement said.

In response, the UK government said France will deploy a “surge team” of 45 officers to the western beaches of France in the coming weeks, building on a deal signed in April to curb unauthorised small boat crossings in the English Channel.

“The progress we have seen this summer shows what can be achieved when the UK and France work together,” Burnham said.

The British prime minister is also seeking closer post-Brexit cooperation with Europe in a bid to boost sluggish domestic growth.

He has said Britain must be “bolder” in getting closer to the EU but has refused to scrap his predecessor’s rejection of rejoining the bloc’s single market or customs union and returning to its internal freedom of movement rules.

Complicating matters is concern that the EU’s Made in Europe agenda, which seeks to protect the steel industries of states in the 27-nation bloc, could harm Britain’s struggling steel sector.

“The Prime Minister set out how the Made in Europe agenda could pose significant challenges for UK industry,” a UK government spokesperson said.

Macron said it was a “very important moment” for relations between the two countries, adding he was “here with a willingness and a commitment to get closer and closer”.

On the subject of defence, Downing Street said the leaders discussed the next steps on establishing local assembly lines in Ukraine for the long-range missile, SCALP, which uses British technology, and reflected on the successful Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv last week.

articles.title: Isro’s GSLV-F17 successfully places EOS-05 Earth observation satellite in geosynchronous orbit
articles.summary: India News: SRIHARIKOTA: The Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) successfully launched EOS-05, India’s first imaging satellite designed to operate from a ge.
articles.body: SRIHARIKOTA: The Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) successfully launched EOS-05, India’s first imaging satellite designed to operate from a geosynchronous orbit, aboard GSLV-F17 in the early hours of Friday.The 51.7-metre-tall, 420.5-tonne, three-stage rocket lifted off from the second launch pad at Sriharikota at 2.55am and placed the around 2,367kg Earth observation satellite in its intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit.This was the 19th GSLV flight. GSLV-F17 had a S139 solid core with four L40H liquid strap-ons, a GL40HT liquid second stage and a CUS15 indigenous cryogenic upper stage, besides a four-metre composite ogive payload fairing.EOS-05 was injected into a geosynchronous transfer orbit. It will eventually achieve a nominal perigee of 170km, apogee of 28,934km and inclination of 19.28 degrees. The satellite will be moved to the final orbit through a series of manoeuvres using onboard thrusters.Isro chairman V Narayanan said the rocket injected the satellite in the intended orbit precisely. This is the 107th launch from Sriharikota and 19th GSLV flight. The chairman addressed from the mission control complex post launch."From launching 1536kg payload in the first GSLV launch, the chairman said the rocket has carried the heaviest payload in its history at 2367kg. We gradually improved the performance of the vehicle by optimising the structural mass and improving propulsion system. The satellite is India's first dedicating imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit. It will provide strategic data."The chairman also said Isro will have six more launches this financial year including navigation satellite NVS-03 and Gaganyaan first uncrewed mission.India had 21 operational Earth observation satellites as of February 2026. Of these, most are in low-Earth or sun-synchronous polar orbits, while India’s geostationary-orbit Earth observation capability is currently represented by the meteorological satellites INSAT-3D, INSAT-3DR and INSAT-3DS. EOS-05 is India’s first imaging satellite to operate from geosynchronous orbit.The launch was the first GSLV mission since GSLV-F16 successfully placed the joint Nasa-Isro NISAR Earth observation satellite in a 743km sun-synchronous orbit on July 30, 2025. Friday’s launch was Isro’s second orbital mission of 2026. The first, PSLV-C62 carrying EOS-N1 and other payloads on Jan 12, failed following an anomaly towards the end of the rocket’s third-stage flight.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump raises doubts over support for Britain in Falklands dispute with Argentina
articles.summary: BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — U.S.
articles.body: BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — U.S. President Donald Trump raised doubts about whether the United States would support Britain in another conflict over the Falkland Islands in an interview with a British broadcaster aired Thursday, injecting new tension into the long-standing dispute over the British-controlled archipelago also claimed by Argentina. Trump’s comments came as his ideological ally, Argentine President Javier Milei, prepared to deliver a televised national address about what his government has described as diplomatic progress over the islands that lie about 480 kilometers (300 miles) off Argentina’s coast in the South Atlantic. When asked in an interview with British television channel GB News whether the U.S. would “come to the aid” of Britain in a new conflict over the territory, Trump avoided answering directly. “Well, look, I was there when they had the first war,” Trump said of the 10-week conflict that erupted in April 1982, when Argentina’s waning military dictatorship invaded the islands and then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher sent British naval forces across the Atlantic to retake them. The war killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders. “That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well,” Trump added. “You took it back pretty strongly.” He then pivoted to complaints that Britain has not provided sufficient support for the U.S.-led bombing campaign against Iran. It wasn’t the first time the Trump administration had drawn a connection between Britain’s claim to the remote islands and its refusal to participate in the U.S. war on Iran: An internal Pentagon email reported in April raised the prospect of Washington reconsidering its position on the archipelago as one possible way to punish NATO allies that declined to join the Iran war. “Your country’s not doing well,” he said of Britain. “Your country was not there to help me.” Trump recalled Britain’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer, telling him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign. “It was pretty sad, the whole thing,” he said. For decades, successive U.S. administrations have remained neutral on the competing Argentine and British sovereignty claims over the Falklands while recognizing Britain’s de facto administration of the islands. Any departure from that position would be a major diplomatic affront and inflame already high trans-Atlantic tensions. Trump had already fueled speculation about a possible shift in U.S. policy on Monday when asked whether his administration was reviewing its stance on the islands. “I always review every position,” Trump replied. “That’s just one of many.” Milei, a free-market libertarian who has struggled to prove his nationalist credentials and previously been criticized for a lack of support for the cause, welcomed Trump’s comment, declaring that “something major happened regarding the most sacred cause we Argentines have.” Asked earlier this week about Milei’s planned address, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s spokesman, Tom Wells, said the British government’s position was “long-standing and unwavering.” He pointed to a 2013 referendum in which the roughly 4,000 people living in the Falkland Islands voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining a British overseas territory. “Sovereignty rests with the U.K., and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount,” Wells said. “The U.K.’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.” Argentina maintains that it inherited sovereignty over the islands from its former colonizer, Spain, and that Britain has illegally occupied them since 1833. The Falklands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, still carry enormous political and symbolic weight as one of the few causes that unite the deeply divided country. Argentine patriotic fervor over the islands flared most recently during this year’s World Cup, when players celebrated their semifinal victory over England by displaying a banner declaring “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” — “The Malvinas are Argentine.”

articles.title: California woman who served a decade in prison for killing a partner will now serve 36 more for murdering her wife
articles.summary: The California woman who fled to Mexico after fatally stabbing her wife, a captain with the state’s wildland firefighting agency, was sentenced this week to 36 years to life in prison, officials said.
articles.body: The California woman who fled to Mexico after fatally stabbing her wife, a captain with the state’s wildland firefighting agency, was sentenced this week to 36 years to life in prison, officials said. Yolanda Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty last month to second-degree murder in the Feb. 17, 2025, death of Rebecca Marodi, 49, at the couple’s home in Ramona, northeast of San Diego, the county’s district attorney said in a statement. Yolanda Marodi previously pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter in the death of an estranged partner in 2003 and served roughly a decade in prison. Yolanda and Rebecca Marodi’s marriage of roughly two years was deteriorating when Yolanda Marodi stabbed her wife roughly two dozen times, the district attorney’s office said. Some of the events of Feb. 17, 2025, were captured in grim security camera video from the couple’s patio, according to an affidavit in support of an arrest warrant. When a bloodied Rebecca Marodi told her wife that she didn’t want to die, Yolanda Marodi responded, “You should have thought about that before.” Roughly a week earlier, the affidavit states, Rebecca Marodi had told her wife she planned on ending their marriage. In a text message cited in the affidavit, Yolanda Marodi told someone that she hurt Rebecca Marodi after learning that the relationship was over and her wife said she’d met someone else. Yolanda Marodi was captured in Mexicali, just south of the U.S. border, on March 22, 2025. During Wednesday’s sentencing hearing, Rebecca Marodi’s mother said it had been “the privilege of a lifetime” to be her parent. “In the face of the greatest darkness, I have stood strong to receive justice for my amazing, beautiful, strong daughter,” said Lorena Marodi, who found her daughter’s body and called 911. “Every morning when I wake, the image of my baby girl lying on the floor with stab wounds to her back and lifeless haunts me,” she said. “Despite the horrific violence bestowed upon Becky, I refuse to allow Yolanda’s darkness to consume me.”

articles.title: Tougher than Everest rescues: Inside Nepal's biggest airlift
articles.summary: South Asia News: Trishuli Bazaar: With roads and bridges severed across Rasuwa and Nuwakot after the Aug 26 Bhote Koshi-Trishuli flood, helicopters became the main res.
articles.body: Trishuli Bazaar: With roads and bridges severed across Rasuwa and Nuwakot after the Aug 26 Bhote Koshi-Trishuli flood, helicopters became the main rescue lifeline, airlifting more than 4,000 people in hundreds of sorties through a narrow gorge in what officials described as possibly Nepal's biggest such operation.Pilots said the missions were tougher than Everest-season flying, with wrong coordinates, landing spots buried under mud, crowded skies, drones and false rescue alerts complicating operations.Talking to TOI at Maithili Barracks, where choppers were taking off and landing in Trishuli Bazaar, Captain Bimal Sharma of Simrik Air said Everest flights, despite the altitude, were more predictable. "Even during the climbing season on Everest, it's still busy, but there's a clear goal of where to go and what to do." Here, he said, coordinates often did not match and pilots sometimes reached places where the landing ground itself had vanished. "We have to search around. In some places where we were asked to land, there was no place to do that."At times, over a dozen helicopters operated simultaneously between Trishuli and the Tibet border. There was no separate airport in the flood-hit area, leaving pilots to work in effectively uncontrolled airspace once inside the gorge. Pilots devised their own rules - keeping left in valleys, announcing positions and maintaining altitude gaps.Captain Maniraj Lama of Kailash Helicopter said the missions changed by the day. Initially, choppers carried doctors and rescuers in and survivors out. They then shifted to food and relief drops; later, as bodies began decomposing at inaccessible sites, crews started lifting some by longline beneath the helicopter.Drones added another hazard. Civil aviation authority of Nepal joint spokesperson Gyanendra Bhul said pilots relied on visual separation and direct communication. "Right now, the biggest challenge for helicopters there is from those drones," he said.False alerts became a recurring drain on flying time. Old and unverified videos kept circulating for days, repeatedly sending helicopters and drones towards places where nobody was found. After one claim that people were stranded in forests around Ghattekhola, national emergency operations centre chief Phanindra Prasad Poudel said, "We even had a helicopter hold the area for 19 minutes. We also monitored it with drones. But nothing was found there."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Michigan farmer bought back the 131 acres his family had lost over the decades; in 2026, he sold the development rights so the land can never be broken up for housing
articles.summary: US News: John Boyer grew up surrounded by the rolling fields of corn, oats and wheat that once belonged to his family in East Jordan, Michigan. Decades later, .
articles.body: John Boyer grew up surrounded by the rolling fields of corn, oats and wheat that once belonged to his family in East Jordan, Michigan. Decades later, after the 131-acre property had changed hands several times outside the family, Boyer made the decision to buy it back.For Boyer, the purchase was about more than owning farmland. He felt a personal responsibility to bring the property back into the family and continue farming it, while ensuring that development would not gradually encroach on the agricultural community.“For any farmer, everything’s personal,” Boyer was quoted as saying by Bridge Michigan. “Every piece of property, every stone you pick up, you spend countless hours out there.”Now, Boyer has taken another significant step to protect the land. In 2026, he sold the future development rights to the Little Traverse Conservancy through a conservation easement, meaning the property can no longer be divided and developed for housing even if ownership changes in the future.Protecting the land from being broken upUnder the conservation easement, Boyer continues to own the 131 acres. However, the Little Traverse Conservancy holds the development rights, restricting future residential and commercial development on the property.The protection remains in place even if Boyer eventually transfers the land to his children or sells it to another owner.For Boyer, the decision was driven by a fear that the property could one day be divided into smaller parcels and sold for development.“Then suddenly a productive farm field or ground is gone, and it’s gone for generations,” Boyer said. “It’s gone forever.”His decision comes at a time when farmland across the United States is expected to change hands on a large scale in the coming decades. Farmers are increasingly weighing the value of their land against pressures from rising property prices, climate change and an aging farming population.Michigan farmland is under growing pressureAccording to the most recent US Department of Agriculture farm census, Michigan had about 9.5 million acres devoted to farming in 2022, roughly a quarter of the state. That was down from approximately 9.8 million acres in 2017.Farmland owned by farmers fell by about 208,000 acres, or 3.6%, over the same period, while leased and rented farmland also declined.At the same time, the value of farmland has continued to rise. USDA data cited in the report shows Michigan farmland was valued at about $6,800 per acre last year, a 7.8% increase from 2024 and higher than the national increase of 4.3%.That creates a complicated situation for farmers who own large amounts of land.“It’s a matter of trying to figure out what exactly is going to be the best fit for everybody’s situation. And there’s a lot of pressure. There’s a lot of money,” said Jon LaPorte, a farm business management educator with Michigan State University Extension.Selling development rights instead of selling the farmA conservation easement offers landowners another way to benefit financially from their property without giving up ownership.Joe Graham, chief financial and operating officer for the Little Traverse Conservancy, said the arrangement allows farmers to capture some of the value tied to their land while keeping the property in their hands.“We’re offering them another alternative,” Graham said. “We’re offering a way to capture some of the equity and the value they have in that land without having to sell it and see it leave their ownership.”The conservancy currently protects around 30,000 acres through conservation easements across five counties in northern Michigan and the Upper Peninsula. About 6,000 of those acres are farmland.However, such agreements can be difficult decisions because selling development rights generally provides less money than selling the land outright. As farmland values rise, some owners may wonder whether they are giving up potential future income.“There can be a question of timing. ‘Is this the right thing to do? What might we be foregoing later?’” Graham said.For Boyer, however, preserving the land for future generations outweighed the possibility of making more money from development.‘They don’t make land anymore’Boyer is not alone in worrying about the long-term future of farmland.Rebecca Carlson, a fourth-generation farmer who operates Overlook Orchards in Northport, Michigan, has also watched land fragmentation become a concern. She said aging farmers can sometimes divide property among several children, creating a patchwork of ownership that can threaten multi-generational farms.Carlson and her husband have expanded their own operation from around 200 acres to 1,300 acres in eight years. They have purchased some land and leased other parcels, often from farming families without a younger generation ready to take over.Leasing can allow farmland to remain in agricultural production while giving farmers access to acreage without the enormous costs associated with buying it.Carlson's leases generally run for about 30 years, with annual fees varying according to factors such as location and crop productivity.“It’s a great way to maintain your farming, your farm and grow your farm,” Carlson said. “They don’t make land anymore.”According to the 2022 USDA census, around 39% of Michigan’s agricultural land is leased, a figure that remained unchanged from 2017.Development pressures extend beyond housingResidential construction is not the only force competing for farmland.Michigan's push toward a cleaner electricity grid has also increased interest in agricultural land for renewable energy projects, including solar farms, wind turbines and battery storage facilities.Jon LaPorte said landowners naturally consider where they can obtain the greatest value from their property.“From a landowner’s perspective, they’ve got bills to pay the same as a farmer, and they’re looking at situations of, ‘Where can I get the most value?’” LaPorte said.Solar currently accounts for only a small portion of Michigan's USDA prime farmland, with about 0.09% used for solar, according to data cited from the Solar Energy Industries Association. Still, proposed projects have generated opposition in farming communities.In Wexford County, plans for solar panels covering nearly 1,500 acres of farmland sparked concerns this year about development encroaching on productive agricultural ground.Carlson believes renewable energy projects should instead be placed on areas such as parking structures, highway medians and high-rise buildings whenever possible.“Put them in places that make sense,” she said. “Don’t take away our resources to grow our own food.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Flood-swept vehicle plugs tunnel mouth, saves 40 workers
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR: Forty workers trapped 3.5km inside the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project miraculously survived the Aug 26 flood after a vehic.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR: Forty workers trapped 3.5km inside the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project miraculously survived the Aug 26 flood after a vehicle swept in by the torrent got wedged near the tunnel mouth and blocked the worst of the mud and debris from rushing inside.With no siren, no initial walkie-talkie alert and no contact with those outside, they waited nearly 45 minutes before making their way out through sludge and water in a two-and-a-half-hour ordeal.Leelanath Neupane, 53, was working deep inside the tunnel when pieces of wood and muddy water began flowing towards the workers. "We had no idea it was floodwater. There was no information through the emergency siren or the walkie-talkie," he said.The 40 workers moved to higher sections and held on to the gantry structure as the mud rose. Neupane used an iron rod to check its depth before they attempted to move. In places, the rod sank 1.5 metres."We first had to understand whether there was any way to get out," Neupane told TOI.What they did not know then was that a vehicle carried by the flood had been pushed into the tunnel and lodged near its entrance. The jeep acted as an accidental barrier, slowing the flow of debris deeper inside. "If the vehicle had not got stuck in the tunnel, our entire tunnel would have filled with mud," Neupane said.A message finally came over the walkie-talkie, warning that a massive flood had struck outside and asking workers to stay put unless they could safely make their way out. The group decided to move. "We had no option," Neupane said. "We held each other and pulled one another through. At some places we crawled, and at others we walked through the mud and water."The men took nearly two-and-a-half hours to reach the tunnel mouth. What they saw outside left many of them disoriented. "What I saw was beyond anything I had imagined. My body and mind stopped working," Neupane said.Nepal army personnel later moved the group to an army camp in Nuwakot. Neupane said several workers remained in shock even after reaching safety. "When they asked for my details, I could remember my name, but I could not recall my phone number or company card number properly," he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Golden retrievers to gather at the breed's ancestral Highland home
articles.summary: The last event held at Guisachan House in the Highlands involved almost 500 dogs.
articles.body:
A mass gathering of golden retrievers and their owners is to be held at the ancestral home of the breed in July 2028.

The event will mark 160 years since the first golden retriever puppies were born at Guisachan House in Glen Affric, near Cannich, in the Highlands.

Meetings to celebrate the breed have been held in different formats by the Golden Retriever Club of Scotland since the late 1990s, with larger events taking place since 2006.

A gathering held at Guisachan in 2023 involved almost 500 dogs from 12 countries .

The Golden Retriever Club of Scotland said a date for the 2028 gathering would be announced later.

Golden retrievers were bred by aristocrat Sir Dudley Marjoribanks, who wanted a gun dog suited to Scottish Highland terrain.

The first litter was born in 1868 to a Tweed water spaniel, a breed now extinct, and yellow wavy-coated retriever.

The puppies were called Primrose, Cowslip and Crocus. Some histories of the breed report the litter having four pups.

More than 40 years later in 1913, the golden retriever was officially recognised as a breed by The Kennel Club, the UK's largest organisation concerned with dog health, welfare and training.

Guisachan House had fallen into ruin by the 1960s.

articles.title: Visitors to get a glimpse inside Bernat Klein studio
articles.summary: The building near Selkirk has been called one of the most significant modernist buildings in Scotland.
articles.body:
The dilapidated studio of renowned textile designer Bernat Klein is to open its doors to the public for the first time since a consortium stepped in to save it from ruin last year.

The group secured the site near Selkirk in the Borders at auction and now has ambitious plans to bring it back into use at a cost of more than £3m.

Visitors are being offered a chance to see the building at the very start of the process of bringing it back to life as part of two Doors Open Days this weekend.

It has a special focus on the modernist work of Peter Womersley who designed the studio and also Klein's nearby home at High Sunderland and the cantilevered stand at Gala Fairydean Rovers' Netherdale ground.

A-listed former textile studio sells for £279,000

The Bernat Klein Studio Coalition - made up of the Bernat Klein Foundation (BKF), the National Trust for Scotland and the Scottish Historic Buildings Trust (SHBT) - was set up to save the building from ruin.

The first phase of work will aim to secure the property, which has been on the Buildings at Risk Register since 2002 and is in a severely dilapidated state.

Once completed, the coalition plans to return The Studio to its original use as a design studio, as well as providing a base for the BKF and its exhibitions, workshops and talks.

The public will get a chance to see the current condition of the building this Saturday and Sunday - and the scale of the task ahead.

Dr Samuel Gallacher, SHBT director, said: "The Bernat Klein Studio, designed by architect Peter Womersley, is one of the most significant modernist buildings in Scotland, yet for more than 20 years it has sat empty and out of use.

"Opening the doors, even for a handful of tours, as part of our National Lottery Heritage Fund project to save the building, reminds people that the Studio belongs to Scotland's story and has a future ahead of it.

"It has earned a real affection, locally and internationally, and we wanted people to see it as it is today, at the very start of its restoration, so they can feel a part of our longer-term project to bring it back to life."

Klein, who died in 2014, collaborated with major European fashion houses such as Dior to design some of the most beautiful textiles of the 20th Century.

His studio was built as a workspace for design, weaving and exhibiting samples.

It lies adjacent to his home, High Sunderland , which was built by Womersley in 1958 and is also a listed building.

articles.title: Experts fear toll could cross 2015 quake of 8.8k
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR: Three days have passed since the last reported live rescue from Nepal's flood-hit hydropower belt, while mud-filled tunnels remain th.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR: Three days have passed since the last reported live rescue from Nepal's flood-hit hydropower belt, while mud-filled tunnels remain the biggest hope for hundreds still missing. With 1,280 people confirmed dead and another 5,624 were unaccounted for across Nepal and Tibet - a combined 6,904 - experts fear the final toll could surpass the nearly 8,800 killed in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake.The last reported rescues from the hydropower belt came on Aug 31. Nepal's national disaster risk reduction and management authority said in its 7pm update Thursday that 1,259 bodies had been recovered and 5,083 people remained missing.Across the border, China reported 21 deaths and 541 missing in Tibet, taking the official two-country count to 1,280 dead and 5,624 missing. But the Tibetan toll remained difficult to independently assess. Reporters Without Borders described the region as a "de facto information black hole".Bijay M Bhattarai, secretary of Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal, told TOI that an earlier casualty projection relied "strictly on official state registries, tourist visa logs and formal corporate HR rosters" and therefore excluded "undocumented populations of riverbed squatter settlements, illegal sand miners and transient transport workers." That gap mattered along Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor, where daily-wage loaders, miners, labourers, drivers and riverside settlers often lived outside formal employment or residence records, he said. A labour-rights organiser told TOI, "The Trishuli gorge doesn't run on formal employment contracts."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iran prefers conflict with US over peace to suppress internal uprising, human rights activist warns
articles.summary: A human rights activist says Iran's regime fears its own population more than U.S. airstrikes, using Strait of Hormuz friction for survival.
articles.body: Regime leaders in Iran are more content to see continued confrontation with the United States and its Gulf neighbors rather than pursuing peace in an effort to keep their disenchanted population at bay, one expert says. U.S. forces have launched airstrikes against Iran in recent days following a brief pause in hostilities amid renewed flare-ups in the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran isn't as concerned about military action against the country, but rather discontent among Iranians, Dr. Majid Sadeghpour, a human rights activist and the political director of the Organization of Iranian-American Communities, told Fox News Digital. TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS Sadeghpour noted that U.S. officials offered guarantees to Tehran that provided a pathway to peace for Iran. "You get America to give you a guarantee that it wouldn't seek regime change. Nevertheless, they still attacked ships afterward," Sadeghpour said. "They still attacked our bases in Jordan and Bahrain. So that speaks to the fact that the real threat to the regime is not the bombs from outside, but rather the population uprising." INSIDE TEHRAN: IRANIANS DESCRIBE IRGC'S BRUTAL RULE, POVERTY — ASK TRUMP TO 'STAY THE COURSE' "For a regime that's militarized and requires friction, its survival now depends on that friction," he added. Iran has experienced major uprisings in recent years driven by economic collapse, high inflation, and deep discontent with the regime's strict religious interpretation of Islam. In addition, the Iranian government has suppressed anti-government riots and protests with deadly force and arbitrary arrests and detention, according to human rights observers. The war with the U.S. helps the regime, Sadeghpour said, by refocusing the Iranian public's attention elsewhere. Meanwhile, Iran has continued to target commercial ships in the strait in violation of an agreement not to do so, Vice President JD Vance said Thursday. IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP "The Iranians are doing what the Iranians do," Vance said. "I think that they're losing their capabilities by the day. I think they're realizing… that their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone, and it's a diminishing asset." In order to effect regime change, the U.S. should focus its efforts on the Iranian population, said Sadeghpour, because Iranian leaders will likely drag out the conflict with the U.S. for as long as they can. "The regime is thinking about the day, the hour after the exhausted population gets calm, and will immediately look around, 'how am I going to get rid of this regime? And who's going to help me do that?' And so that is what the regime is afraid of," he said. TRUMP REVIVES IRAN REGIME CHANGE SPECULATION WITH CRYPTIC CALL FOR PEOPLE TO 'RISE UP' Meanwhile, President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he isn't focused on bringing Tehran to the bargaining table, saying he "couldn't care less" if Iran signs a "worthless" agreement. articles.title: Pig kidney works in human body for 271 days - is this the future of organ transplants?
articles.summary: A man has lived for a record nine months with a transplanted pig kidney while waiting for a human transplant.
articles.body:
A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.

Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.

The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.

But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.

Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.

In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list.

Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis.

"I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.

But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel".

"Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

Pigs are seen as the ideal animal for xenotransplantation. Their organs are roughly the right size and there have been years of experience farming them.

But you cannot just pop down to the farm and take a kidney from a pig and put it into a person. The human body would immediately identify the organ as foreign and launch a devastating immune assault that would destroy the kidney. It would turn black in minutes as holes are ripped in every cell and the organ clots from the inside.

So researchers have developed Yucatan miniature pigs that have gone through 69 genomic modifications to "humanise" their organs.

These modifications strip out some features of pig cells that our immune system spots and attacks; add some human DNA that acts like camouflage netting to help hide the pig tissue from the immune system and further tweaks disable viruses that hide inside pig DNA to prevent infection.

Are pigs the future of organ transplants?

Andrews had end stage kidney disease as a result of type 2 diabetes and his kidney's were failing.

He was 66 years old when he had the xenotransplant on January 25, 2025.

The transplanted pig kidney worked immediately, according to details just published in the Lancet medical journal .

The kidney continued to function for 271 days until it was removed in October that year. Tim then needed dialysis for 82 days until he had an organ from a donor in January of this year. That organ has been working well.

Dr Leonardo Riella, from the centre for transplantation sciences at Mass General Brigham said the shortage of organs available for transplant meant " we are in a crisis".

"We are working really hard to bring hope and we truly feel that xenotransplantation can be an alternative for patients who don't have a living donor where we could potentially bypass dialysis and get them to a transplant," he said.

Man who received first pig kidney transplant dies

There were early signs Andrews' organ was being rejected by the immune system, but that was successfully treated by adjusting his medication.

However, after around six months the blood vessels in the kidney started to become damaged and the organ inflamed and then it started to fail.

It is not clear exactly why as there were no signs of antibodies attacking the pig kidney.

In their Lancet write-up the doctors state: "This case illustrates both the promise and the remaining challenges of clinical kidney xenotransplantation."

articles.title: AI tools that take notes for GPs could miss vital information, study suggests
articles.summary: Researchers said the tools - which record consultations - could miss vital things like a patient's facial expressions or emotional state.
articles.body:
AI tools that are used to take medical notes from patients could miss vital information and lead to medical staff being deskilled, according to new research.

The tools, called ambient AI scribes, are used by about 40% of GPs in the UK. The scribes listen to conversations between doctors and patients and convert the speech to text, generating written notes and letters.

Academics at University of Edinburgh reviewed cases involving the scribes and found the tech had some positives, such as allowing clinicians to focus on complex tasks.

However, they also said patients could be less forthcoming if they knew they were being recorded and found instances where doctors did not recognise their notes.

The findings are peer-reviewed and have been published in the British Medical Journal's digital health and AI publication .

The report concluded AI scribes can help with administrative work but more research needs to be done to understand how they work in specific healthcare settings and how their design supports both patients and clinicians.

It comes months after the BBC heard from doctors in the West Midlands, who said their workload had been significantly cut by using the transcription tool Heidi.

At one clinic in Dudley, the tool was credited with reducing a backlog of posting patient letters from six months to 14 days.

One of the key findings by the University of Edinburgh was that although AI tools can help capture what patients say, they can sometimes miss important aspects of consultations - such as facial expressions, gestures and emotional state.

The report said AI summaries tend to prioritise clinical information, which can come at the expense of the patients' stories and experiences of their illness.

It was also found that patients may be hesitant to reveal sensitive information - such as substance abuse, domestic abuse or mental health struggles - when they know the consultation is being recorded and processed by AI.

Researchers also highlighted that manual notetaking serves important functions for clinicians in their reasoning and reflection on what the patient has said.

Their report said using AI scribes could result in "cognitive offloading" for clinicians - which means the tools take on some of their mental effort.

This can have benefits, the report said, as clinicians can spent their efforts having more meaningful conversations with patients or concentrating on complex tasks.

However, it also said the tools can reduce memory recall and skill development and highlighted instances where clinicians do not recognise their own notes or remember the patient the next time they see them.

The researchers concluded that in designing these systems, they must preserve the patient's voice rather than overwrite it.

They also said more work needs to be done to understand the medium and long-term use of these AI tools in specific settings and emerging risks, particularly for tools used in countries with different healthcare systems to where the AI tools have been built.

Dr Lucas Seuren, of the University of Edinburgh's centre for biomedicine, self and society, said: "Many clinicians are excited about ambient AI scribes, because they promise to cut down on paperwork.

"But the experiences of patients are poorly considered, and there are real risks that the patients' stories are lost.

"This can further disadvantage people who already face marginalisation in health and social care services."

articles.title: 'Didn't benefit country': Kenya ousts Tata Chemicals
articles.summary: Rest of World News: NAIROBI: Kenya's President William Ruto said on Thursday he had ordered Tata Chemicals to stop its operations as its presence had failed to benefit th.
articles.body: NAIROBI: Kenya's President William Ruto said on Thursday he had ordered Tata Chemicals to stop its operations as its presence had failed to benefit the country.Fresh investors would take over its mining rights for minerals that are processed into soda ash.Ruto said he asked a unit of the Mumbai-based company "to pack and go" because it has been exporting soda ash rather than using it at local facilities to make glass and chemicals. "That Tata company... had that contract for 100 years yet it has not built anything in Kajiado," Ruto said of the county that's home to Lake Magadi, from which the firm has extracted minerals to make soda ash for two decades. "They take our resource to India and other places."Kenya has produced the resource since 1911 and Tata bought the operation from Brunner Mond Ltd in 2005. Ruto's statement refers to the century-long concessions originally granted to its predecessor. Tata Chemicals declined to comment.Ruto’s remarks came five weeks after Kenya’s mining ministry directed Tata Chemicals Magadi Ltd to suspend operations, citing its failure to make royalty payments and to meet other regulatory requirements. “We have said we will bring a new company and... they should put a big glass company here in Kajiado. And another company to make chemicals here in Kajiado. Are we slaves to other people?” “Come what may, because they have been unable to do what is required, I have told them to pack and go,” Ruto said.Local reports said the opposition slammed Ruto’s decision, accusing him of ousting Tata Chemicals to bring in other companies associated with his govt allies to explore oil in the area. Democracy for Citizens Party said 500 direct employees and thousands of support workers had been rendered jobless overnight due to the closure.Kajiado governor Joseph Ole Lenku said the mining rights expired in 2023. “Those who we will licence to extract the resource must build a huge processing facility here to produce glass. They should build a big factory to produce chemicals here,” he told supporters at a rally.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
